## Original Article

## Incidences, Predictors, and Clinical Outcomes of Acute and Late Stent Malapposition Detected by Optical Coherence Tomography After Drug-Eluting Stent Implantation

Eui MD*= Byeong-Keuk Kim; MD* Young-Guk MD; Dong-Ho Shin, MD; Jung-Sun Kim, MD; Donghoon Choi, MD; Yangsoo Jang, MD; Myeong-Ki MD, Im, Ko, Hong,

PhD

Background We investigated the incidences, predictors, and clinical outcomes of acute and late stent malapposition detected by coherence tomography (OCT) after drug-eluting stent implantation. optical

Conclusions\_Acute, late-persistent;  and late-acquired stent malapposition had relatively high incidences but different predictors. The clinical outcome of stent malapposition was favorable. (Circ Cardiovasc Interv. 2014,7:00-00.)

Methods and Results We analyzed the OCT images from 351 patients with 356 lesions who received poststent and follow up OCT examinations. Acute stent malapposition was observed in 629 of lesions. Approximately half of the acute stent malappositions were located within the edges of the stents. Severe diameter stenosis, calcified lesions, and stents were independent predictors of acute stent malapposition: Follow-up OCT examinations were performed 175+60 after drug-eluting stent implantation: Thirty-one percent of lesions with acute stent malapposition remained malapposed (late-persistent stent malapposition) and were typically (729) located within the edges of the stent. The location within the stent and the volume of acute stent malapposition were independent predictors of late-persistent stent malapposition: Acute stent malapposition with a volume >2.56 mm? differentiated late-persistent stent malapposition from resolved acute stent malapposition. Late-acquired stent malapposition was detected in 159 of all lesions and was usually (61%) located within the stent body. Late-acquired stent malapposition was more frequently associated with plaquelthrombus prolapse on poststent OCT images (70% versus 42%; P<o.001). Clinical events, including cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction; and stent thrombosis, did not occur in patients with late stent malapposition during the follow-up period of 28.6110.3 months after drug-eluting stent implantation. long days edges

Yoronary stent malapposition is of stent 'strut from the intimal surface of the coronary arterial wall without involvement of side branches In the era of eluting stents (DESs), late-acquired stent malapposition is well-recognized problem in interventional cardiology because it may constitute potent substrate for late stent thrombosis.'-3 The incidence of late-acquired stent malapposition was reported to be as high as 259 in patients with acute myocar dial infarction. In addition; predictors of late-acquired stent malapposition include plaque or thrombus absorption or tive vascular remodeling. '5,6 Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) imaging was used to detect stent malapposition in previous studies. IVUS may not completely detect stent malapposition because of limited axial resolution (100-200 um) or stent related (OCT) with a higher resolution (12-18 um) may detect stent malapposition with greater accuracy. ## Methods

Patients   who received implantation of DESs for de novo coronary lesions between January 2009 and December 2011 with poststent and follow-up OCT were identified from the OCT registry database of our institute. Exclusion criteria included the following (1) the DES was implanted for left main coronary disease; (2) there were overlapping DESs implanted in the lesion; (3) the clinical follow-up period after DES implantation was <1 year; (4) follow-up OCT was performed >1 year after DES implantation; and (5) the OCT image had poor quality Ultimately; 351 patients with 356 lesions were enrolled in this study. the same study period, there were 3235 patients (3587 lesions During
